subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, March 29, consideration of the motion of Hon. Mitchell Sharp, (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Tuesday evening I called the presentation of the Minister of Finance, which we are again debating today, a dead end budget. I repeat that, Mr. Speaker. It has no goals or directions.
This budget does little to control inflation. It virtually ignores the country's international payments deficit. It leaves many injustices uncorrected. It does nothing for the forgotten pensioners. It maintains mountains of paper work for the bureaucracy. It will reduce incentives, and it does nothing to develop the long term goals of the country's destiny.
This is a bureaucratic budget which is confusing, full of paper forms and even paper clips, one might say. It starts with the assumption that you can get away with anything if you confuse the people and if you confuse business enough. In other words, Mr. Speaker, and I am only interjecting this in a facetious manner, you can play any tune on the piano if you hum loudly enough.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You have to have a piano.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Sir, I believe this is a budget involving economic myopia. Only a few short months ago we were in an election campaign. We heard many promises from the present leaders on the government benches. They said "Give us a majority and we shall do wonders".
I would remind these hon. gentlemen of a few of those promises. I would ask the Minister of Finance what provision has been made for the skating rink in Vancouver. What about the $1 million for Digby harbour, or the millions more promised for housing? What provision has been made for the causeways, or I suppose now one might say "pause
April 1, 1966	COMMONS
ways"? What about the $25 million for Cape Breton coal, the dams which have been promised all over the country, the undertaking to provide home mail delivery in small towns, the study of fish which was to be made in Newfoundland, or the $100 million promised for road building in the Yukon-a promise which, incidentally, did not have the effect desired by the government on election day? These are all things which were promised but for which I see no provision made.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
I would be lax in my duty, I feel, if I did not congratulate the minister on his success in the dumping of his predecessor's budget items and the complete reversal of earlier policies both good and bad. "Troubled Canada", Mr. Gordon wrote. "Troubled Walter", Mr. Sharp says. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) lowered income taxes. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) raised them. The hon. member for Davenport put an 11 per cent sales tax on production machinery. The Minister of Finance is timidly removing it. The hon. member for Davenport made much of his billion dollar Canada Development Corporation, which was to have done wonders. The Minister of Finance has forgotten all about it. In fact I suggest Mr. Sharp has forgotten all about Mr. Gordon. In less than a year we have seen a complete switch-round in Liberal direction. We are substituting for the 60 days of decision the present minister's stiletto and 365 days of incision.
I should like to put on record a few extracts to show what sections of the press think about this budget. First I would quote from an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Daily Star of March 30:
Mr. Sharp's budget is a shotgun affair which applies to the whole country without regard to regional differences. It ignores the fact that while some regions, such as Ontario have been experiencing a boom verging on inflation, the good times have hardly touched the maritimes and eastern Quebec, where unemployment rates remain far higher than in central Canada. In these depressed areas, the anti-inflation budget could be a recession one.
Then I would quote one or two passages from Le Devoir by Mr. Claude Ryan. I do not think I should burden the house with my French; I have had the passages translated into English and I will read them in English.
While there should be no hesitation in accepting Mr. Sharp's basic outlook in this connection we may well ask ourselves, however, if he has indeed chosen the proper means for the realization of his purposes.
DEBATES	3725
The Budget-Mr. Monteith
In the case of the federal government we should have been able to contemplate a severe reduction not only of spending in respect of construction, but also of the entire spending estimates. Instead of that Mr. Sharp was content to announce a very inconsequential 10 per cent cut in Ottawa's building program. A reduction of approximately $35 millions in total expenses totalling nearly $9 billion is obviously but a drop in the ocean. It may well be wondered what actual effect such a timid move will have on the decisions of other governments as well as on the actual performance of the economy generally. If the federal government really had wanted to set an example it has proceeded very timidly indeed.
Again:
They take no account whatever either of the variety of capital investment problems as they apply to various types of industry nor of the different levels of industrial development as achieved by one area as opposed to another.
And here is an interesting passage:
A year ago the floodgates had been thrown wide open to allow for free play of individual initiative. Since the people were to be called upon to vote they had to be treated as pleasantly as possible. One year later we find ourselves, once again, in the position in which we were before Mr. Gordon's election budget. Whatever Mr. Sharp may say, this is a difference which cannot be explained away entirely by changes in economic circumstances. Its explanation must be looked for, to some extent, in the opportunism of the party in power. If we are now returning to soundly based austerity it is simply because there is no fear of early elections.
Incidentally I think I should put on record the concluding sentence in this editorial:
Unfortunately, nobody thought of encouraging Canadians to invest in their own future, which is perhaps driving short term caution a little iar.
These two editorials give a concise picture of how inept this budget really is. I claim it is leading Canada down the proverbial garden path. I would commend the minister on accepting at least a few elements of the Progressive Conservative party's program. Naturally it is heartening to any political party to find its opponents adopting some of its "policies for people." I refer to the announcement by the Minister of Agriculture offering $4 per hundredweight for industrial milk, which of course was in our program. I refer also to the decision to treat potash solution mining in the same way as any other type of mining for tax purposes. This too was one of our policies. But why did it take so long? Now that parliament has a new senator from that province the government will be able to keep in touch with the needs of the people out there. This is an important decision for Saskatchewan.
The 11 per cent sales tax has now been removed from certain production machinery,
April 1. 1966

The Budget-Mr. Monteith jigs and moulds, and notice has been given that in one or two years from now it will be reduced and finally eliminated in respect of all production machinery. We hope the minister lives up to this budget undertaking better than his party has lived up to its campaign promises. We deplore the fact that the minister has not gone further in this direction, as our party has suggested.
The president of the Auto Parts Manufacturers Association of Canada emphasized the seriousness of this tax in a statement reported in yesterday's Globe and Mail. His industry is being told to compete with the United States giants which are not required to pay a comparable sales tax. Not only do Canadian firms have to meet competition from these bigger, low cost United States firms, but they have to pay an 11 per cent tax as well. The Minister of Industry told them "Have courage to expand." The manufacturers wanted to know why the Minister of Industry had not talked to the Minister of Finance. As the president of the manufacturers association said in the Globe and Mail: "When a government advocates free trade and then does something like this, you just wonder where the brains are."
[DOT] (12:00 noon)
We have pressed for the removal of the 11 per cent sales tax on building machinery, supplies and materials. In fact, we were firmly against it from its inception. The minister has said that in the course of a year or two this tax will be wiped out so far as machinery and equipment are concerned. I ask, why not now? His answer, of course, may be twofold, first, that he needs the money and, second, that he is seeking to delay orders for machinery and equipment for a period of time until demand slackens.
I believe the minister and the government have gone about this whole thing backwards. How in the world can the demand be satisfied if the means of producing for that demand are going to be delayed and delayed? I feel encouragement should be given to industry to provide the required facilities to produce so that the demand can be satisfied. I do not believe that the required production facilities needed across Canada should be delayed. We do not want to set this country back. We want to see the demand satisfied.
The minister has been trying to squeeze down the demand and ignores the fact that the government should be encouraging production on the supply side of things. The

Minister has pretended that he has been dealing with inflation while he has only been monkeying around with the economy, which in turn will be self-defeating.
Let me now turn to the items in the budget which are prominent by their absence. Why did the minister not discuss the auto parts agreement when his predecessor boasted so proudly of it only last year?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Because it is on the Order Paper.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We welcome the jobs the agreement may provide but we are concerned that a weak government here in Ottawa will do nothing to stand up for this country's interests. How much of that $50 million in tariff reductions have Canadians received in lower car prices? How are our parts manufacturers getting along? Why are we not told? There is plenty to be discussed in the auto agreement but I think the government does not want to discuss it.
This is quite a different song from last October and November when the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and various other ministers were falling all over themselves with boastful praises. We have heard the good part but now we are hearing the other side. There are many things the government should have done. We had hoped for something for our old age pensioners, and I suggest that the government's flippancy in this respect is a shame and a disgrace.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext: auto parts manufacturers asked the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) to talk to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), I suggest that the Prime Minister talk to the Minister of Finance. The older people of this land are still waiting. Does the government care? I say no, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: There are only four ministers in the house now.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then there are other items like the sales tax on drugs. We promised to remove it. Last year the former minister of finance said he was not acting on it because the Special Committee on Food and Drugs was studying the situation. This year the present minister says that the committee is still studying it but if the committee recommends removal of the tax the government will act. I have never heard such nonsense, Mr. Speaker, asking the committee to make a recommendation and telling it beforehand the effect of anything it might say. We wish the minister would follow the same policy with respect to the Economic Council's program for greater productivity.
There are some temporary measures in the budget. There are the changes in the capital cost allowances but they really mean very little in the over-all picture. They are going to frustrate and confuse immeasurably the plans of the small businessman. I know, having been an auditor for this type of client for many years.
They are also going to hurt the farmer. Yet over all they will do little to change the direction of the economy. Capital cost allowance changes are not going to affect the expansion plans of several large corporations. I think I should mention one or two such as the Steel Company of Canada, General Motors, and MacMillan Bloedell and Powell River. This type of corporation is not going to let depreciation changes affect its plans for the future. If there is any curtailment we believe that it will merely put off still further the day when consumer demand can be met.
The income tax changes mean greater taxes for many Canadians, probably the best proof we have that the government is not going to try for a majority this year. Last year was rather obvious-taxes down, an election. Then the Canada Pension Plan came in and wiped out the difference. Now taxes are up-certainly no election.
To me the income tax changes are meaningless. They do assist the minister in his financing but the amounts involved are not

The Budget-Mr. Monteith going to mean anything. Those who are gaining some minor benefits are going to spend the extra few cents a week, which is all it is going to amount to. Those who are receiving $25,000 and over are not going to let an extra $580 in tax deter them from buying a new car or anything else they may wish. In fact, the $580 could well be savings that would have been reinvested in Canada's future by people in this category. A married person with two children, earning $10,000 a year is going to pay something like $119 extra tax. Here again this is not really going to affect inflation, but we wonder why wage earners making $5,000 and up are being forced to pay more.
There is only one method to meet the problem of inflation and that is to increase supply to meet the demand. Mr. Speaker, if you really want to find something to challenge the willing, scare the daring and frighten the weak, you must try the minister's refundable tax on cash profits. It is not what it looks like; it looks like what it is not. I suggest the minister must have been reading Abe Lincoln when he thought that one up and he got carried away. Lincoln said:
Towering genius disdains a beaten path. It seeks regions hitherto unexplored.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, we see bureaucracy at work. The government is presuming to decide what is good for business and thinks it can do it better than business can decide for itself. I do not believe this is the case.
Let us just examine this 5 per cent refundable tax. Just what does this gimmick mean? I claim it is useless, impractical, unfair and unlikely to achieve the desired results. It is really nothing more than a forced loan to the government so that it can borrow money at 5 per cent, below the current market rate.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
Inflation is expected to continue this year and the tax, therefore, is really a partial confiscation of capital, taken from business now and to be paid back when the dollars are worth less. It will be imposed on companies with no capital spending programs, and it is even possible to doubt that its real purpose is as an anti-inflationary measure. It will apply to any taxpaying corporation including banks, trust companies and companies in the service industry which have virtually no capital spending program. Therefore the tax cannot possibly curtail capital spending so far as these particular companies are concerned. It
April 1, 1966

The Budget-Mr. Monteith means an unfair burden on companies engaged in the exploration for natural resources as it includes depletion allowances in its tax base. This certainly is a field of endeavour which we do not want to curtail.
The minister said that this tax would affect only some 20 per cent of the major companies. I should like to quote from an article in the Financial Post of April 2, this week's issue. It is by Clyde Baxter and reads:
Sharp and his officials are confident most companies are already so advanced in their 1966 planning, and even in many cases for the next year, too, that the great majority will go ahead despite the new regulations.
I think that quotation sets out the whole thing in a nutshell. It is a personal opinion, but I would agree with Mr. Baxter. Most companies of any size have made plans for one, two, three, or more years in advance. Does the minister think for one minute that these large corporations from which he is going to take this refundable tax are going to cease their modernizing plans because of this tax? Surely the minister realizes that large corporations cannot operate that way. Just what is going to happen? Their own money in the form of this tax is going to lie dormant in the minister's hands while they go out to borrow funds to complete their modernizing requirements. It is going to cost them more; they are going to pay more than the five per cent which the minister is going to pay them. Who is going to pay the cost of that extra interest? Naturally, the consumer. It is going to increase the cost of living. It is going to be reflected right down to the consumer level. This again is one of those things that is going to make our industry and particularly our larger industry less competitive both in our foreign markets and in our domestic market.
International companies are going to be tempted to leave funds overseas rather than repatriate them. I could mention a few such as Hiram Walker, Distillers Corporation, Seagram Limited, Moore Corporation, and Massey-Ferguson. The only funds they may wish to bring back to Canada are those sufficient to pay dividends. Why would they bring home funds only to have to pay five per cent of them to the government and receive only five per cent interest? I might point out at this stage that the minister is going to get needed funds at five per cent interest and only yesterday he sold government of Canada treasury bills at a long time high interest rate. June 30 maturities averaged 5.06 per cent and one year ago they were at 3.62 per 
cent; September 30 maturities cost the government 5.30 per cent and a year ago they were 3.73 per cent. This shows how our money is going; it is becoming more expensive. Here is an opportunity for the minister to get money from these companies at five per cent when on the current market he is paying considerably more. These are forced loans that he is going to impose on quite a few of these larger corporations.
I know of one company which has a capital expenditure program of over $100 million which was decided upon two years ago. It is engaged largely in export. Will this move by the minister stop it from completing this program? Will it help them to know that in 1968 there will be no 11 per cent tax on machinery and equipment? Will it help the company to take five per cent of their surplus cash and force them into the market to borrow? The minister is keeping the production costs of this company higher than is necessary in two ways. They are going to have to pay the tax on their new machinery and equipment because they cannot stop in midstream. They are also going to have to pay to the department their five per cent refundable tax and probably borrow at a higher rate of interest to complete their expansion program. This can only increase their cost of production.
Let us look at the consequences of the increased cost of production, namely, increased prices and an increased cost of living to the average Canadian. Let us look at what the government is itself doing. It is reducing its expenditures by something like $35 million. Note that, Mr. Speaker, $35 million out of approximately $9 billion in total federal spending, an infinitesimal percentage. If it believes seriously that it wants to delay construction and expansion in industry, why does it not act more forcibly in its own sphere of activity? The government should take a hard line in curtailing its own spending. Why does it not reduce these budgetary figures? Goodness knows, there are enough areas. I suggest we could wipe out the entire Department of Industry. The government is suggesting that private industry should reduce expenditures but certainly it is not acting responsibly itself in this respect. It is failing to restrain expenditure as it expects the private sectors of our economy to do. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this is typical bureaucratic mentality as exemplified by this Liberal government.
The minister has paid lip service to the Economic Council of Canada. He did this on
April 1. 1966

more than one occasion in his budget speech but then proceeded to act contrary to their advice. He admits this himself. I would like to refer to one sentence in a column by Mr. Fraser Robertson in the Globe and Mail of March 31:
But Mr. Sharp's opinion of the Economic Council is only so-so. He takes from its report the parts he likes, rejects what he does not like, in the manner of a child fussing with its dinner.
I should like to quote a few words from the report of the Bank of Canada. The minister answered a question this morning. I am paraphrasing but I think it was to the effect that the Bank of Canada and the minister are in accord on policies. I do not think this can be accepted.

The output of the economy in 1965 could have been even higher if our productivity performance had been better. The productivity gains which accompanied the reduction in the margin of unused resources over the past year or so have been disappointing.
This next sentence is important.
This underlines the need for emphasis on policies bearing on "the supply side" of the economy which enhance our ability to produce. It is also the case that unemployment is still high in some areas, and output would be greater if the remaining pockets of unused resources were drawn into employment.
At page 11 of the same report the following is stated:
While we must continue to make the best arrangements we can for access to foreign capital to protect ourselves against the possible need for difficult and concentrated adjustments, I believe that
The Budget-Mr. Monteith we should be aiming at a pattern of economic growth which, while providing for full utilization of our resources, involves reduced dependence on net capital inflows. This does not mean that we should adopt inward-looking attitudes. On the contrary it means that we must attach great importance to increasing our ability to compete effectively with foreign producers both in other countries and in Canada. It means that we should be increasingly concerned with maximizing our productivity and industrial efficiency, with up-grading our labour and management skills, and with keeping our costs and prices in line.
This can only be done by concentrating our efforts on satisfying the demand and by concentrating on the supply side, as the governor of the Bank of Canada has said.
I should also like to quote from a pamphlet entitled "Private and Public Investment in Canada, Outlook 1966" published by the authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters). There are one or two statements of interest in this pamphlet. I should like to quote from page 7:
Within the goods producing industries the greatest additional strength appears in the resource based forest and minerals industries where outlays are expected to increase by one-third compared with the 14 per cent rise recorded last year. Of particular significance are the programs currently planned by the mining industry. These involve a doubling of expenditures in iron mines and a similar increase in outlays for potash mines. In addition, spending for facilities for non-ferrous metal mines is expected to rise by about 50 per cent. The added strength in the forest based industries is entirely the result of a further substantial expansion of investment for pulp and paper mills, involving outlays some $120 million greater than those of 1965.
Does the minister want to stop this? These industries help our foreign exchange position; they provide employment and expansion. Expansion means efficiency which in turn means that these companies will then be able to compete in world markets. Surely we want our export industries to be able to compete efficiently in order that we can keep our costs down, which in turn will help our own citizens.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has pointed out that new construction will increase by 12 per cent to reach a level of $9.2 billion and that expenditures for the acquisition of new machinery and equipment will increase by 17 per cent to reach a level of $5.4 billion. If the Minister of Finance wants to lower costs and wants to put the brake on inflation he should remove the 11 per cent tax now so that these companies will not have to pay the 11 per cent on new equipment.

I suggest we want to create supply to satisfy demand. One can only curtail inflation in this way. This is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has to say in this regard:
While in the short run adding to the strong demand and cost pressures already present in the economy, larger capital spending programs, once completed, will substantially increase Canada's productive capacity.
That can be found at page 9 of the pamphlet to which I have referred. That is exactly what we want and that is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggests will happen. He states:
-larger capital spending programs, once completed, will substantially increase Canada's productive capacity.
The Minister of Finance is attempting to put on the brakes and I do not think this should be done. We think our choice is simple. We want to stop the cost of living from rising any further. We think the 11 per cent sales tax on machinery and equipment and building materials increases costs and hurts productivity. We think the refundable tax program is nonsense.
We suggest that we should approach our problems by expanding production, by increasing supply and not by sitting on demand. We do not want our old people to be told that there is something evil about wanting a decent pension or our young people to be told that they must not seek a better education. We do not want our wage earners to be told that they have no right to good wages or our industrialists to be told that they

should shudder at the sight of their own shadows.
It is higher productivity that will put some power back into the wage earners pay envelopes, that will permit industry to pay higher wages, that will keep prices from rising and that will make Canada competitive in world markets. Increasing supply is the road to a higher standard of living and a greater wealth for all Canadians. The governor of the Bank of Canada has said this, the Economic Council has said this and the Department of Trade and Commerce has said this. Why does the Minister of Finance not realize that this is the fact?
We have no confidence in this budget, Mr. Speaker, in that we do not believe it will meet the needs of Canada and its people. Therefore I move:
That all the words after 'that' be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
That the policies of this government have failed to deal constructively and effectively with major national problems facing Canada which require action now to provide policies for adequate incentives to increase productivity, stimulate export trade, to meet the serious and increasing imbalance of international payments, to maintain price stability, and to promote orderly and equitable development and expansion in all areas in the nation.
Mr. Speaker, we are tired of the "little Canada" approach. This is a big land crying out for development. We will never have it if we are afraid.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to the best of my recollection our present Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) is the sixth Minister of Finance whose budget I have had occasion to deal with in this chamber. Ministers of this government seem to have a rather short, if not merry, life, a sort of mayfly life, and we must make the most of this minister while we have him. I have always found that budgets are revealing not merely of the government's policies but also of the outlook on life and society of the minister. I hope the present
April 1, 1966

minister will not take it amiss when I suggest that I find this budget rather grey and cautious, imbued with the spirit of ca'canny which one might expect from someone of his ancestry.
In this budget there is none of that rather engaging, shall I say, "zany" quality of bold improvisation which characterized the budget of one of his predecessors, a budget that was presented with considerable panache. I suppose at this particular juncture in the world's history the question is which of these two courses is the better. In a world which is changing like a kaleidoscope, is it better to mount the steed of enthusiasm and ride off in all directions at once or ride one which stands almost still and hardly moves in any direction? At least we can be sure that the present Minister of Finance will not ride for a fall. His dagger is that he will petrify into an equestrian statue.
In light of the minister's personality, shall I say, his outlook on life, it is understandable that in the welter of conflicting advice which he no doubt has received, particularly in regard to the question of inflation or no inflation, inflationary pressures or no inflationary pressures, he should steer a careful, middle course between the bland, qualified optimism of Dr. Deutsch and the worried pessimism of Mr. Rasminsky. I have noticed that the minister seems to have come down pretty well on the side of the dangers of inflationary pressures.
I have been a bit disturbed by some voices, not particularly bright and rather simple-minded, that have been raised recently which equate the rise in the cost of living index with inflation. It is true enough that rising prices may be an indication of a general inflationary situation, but that is not necessarily so. There are indeed many other circumstances in our economy which will lead to a rise in prices rather than a general inflationary situation. We have such things, for instance, as administered prices which are set by corporations in monopoly and near-monopoly positions without very much regard to costs and with hardly any more concern than what the traffic will bear.
It is very often said that increased wages are the cause of price rises, and of course on occasion this is true; only a fool would deny it. But this is only part of the story. Very often, sir, increased wages impel the employer to adopt much more efficient methods of production and cause a drop in the unit cost of production which does not justify price
The Budget-Mr. C. Cameron increases but nevertheless causes price increases.
In my own province of British Columbia, in the principal industry of that province it is notorious that all wage increases are recouped by the employer with an additional 10 per cent or 15 per cent. It has happened repeatedly year after year, and more often than not the increase in price has taken place before the wage increase. When an employee tries to obtain an increase in wages he is really demanding a larger share of the wealth which he produces, and when employers refuse to grant him that larger share, which they do by maintaining their own profit position by increasing prices, then we get, stemming I suppose, from the wage increase a price increase.
However, Mr. Speaker, at this point there comes the question that we in this party have raised several times this session, namely, the necessity of taking some action with regard to spiralling prices. We have suggested that in co-operation with the provinces there should be a prices review board which could examine these increases, particularly in basic prices, to see whether they were justifiable. I suspect that all that would be required in many instances would be public exposure of the actual situation in any particular industry.
Of course, our minister does not take such a simpleminded view. He presents to us a much more sophisticated approach to the problem of inflation or inflationary pressures and tells us in effect that we are approaching the full utilization of our resources and consequently the danger of inflationary pressures becomes extremely severe.
There are roughly three sections of our resources. One is our natural resources; the second is the industrial plant by which those resources can be transformed into commodities, and the third is our human resources. To the best of my knowledge, neither the minister nor anyone else can tell us what our natural resources are. For one thing, they have not all been explored and for another, of course, their economic utility will depend on changing economic circumstances both in Canada and abroad.
It may be that our industrial equipment is working at full capacity or near full capacity today, but no one has suggested that it is necessarily working in the most efficient manner possible. Indeed, the minister himself in parts of his budget address made suggestions as to means of increasing productivity
April 1, 1966

The Budget-Mr. C. Cameron in our industry, which would indicate that he himself has some doubts whether Canadian industry is as productive as it should be. But there can be no question about the status of our human resources. When the minister tells us that we are approaching the full utilization of all our resources and consequently must be very concerned about the danger of inflation, he blandly ignores our 356,000 unemployed. These are the latest figures I could obtain, as at February 19, seasonally adjusted. Three and a half per cent of our total labour force are unemployed.
It would appear that the minister is prepared to dismiss this particular part of our resources, perhaps justifiably. Perhaps he takes the position that these unemployed are useless as factors of production. It may well be that because of defective education, lack of technical skills or poor physical health arising from long continued poverty, these
356.000	unemployed are actually not capable of being part of our productive force at the present time, that there is no place for them within our industrial economy, that they are in fact a burden upon the rest. To say this may very well be true. Admittedly, it is a very cold-blooded approach to regard human beings in this manner. I shall have something to say later, Mr. Speaker, about this social philosophy that impels us to so regard human beings, a social ethos which narrows man's potentiality, which confines him to the role of a producing and consuming animal. However, this is the way which, in the context of the minister's Budget, we must consider these
356.000	unemployed. We must consider them as people who are at present not valuable assets in the productive forces of our country.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
Now, the minister implies this when he ignores this situation and at the same time tells us we are approaching the limit of utilization of our resources. In fact, he discards them as defective parts of the machine which, as I say, they may very well be. But, sir, I would point out that even if we set aside moral and humane considerations with regard to those who are dismissed from our active society, and I do not think we should do that, this is still a shocking, wasteful extravagance from an economic point of view and one that is simply unsupportable.
If the unemployed are unfit for the purposes of industrial society, and as I say there may very well be a case to be made out for

that, the fact we have had a hard core of unemployment lasting year after year which we are apparently unable to shrink to any appreciable extent would indicate that we have this large corps of people who cannot be fitted into the industrial machinery of our modern society. If that is so, Mr. Speaker, then it seems to me that obviously our task is, before we speak of the full utilization of resources, to sharpen, to polish and reshape these defective parts of our human resources so that they can be fitted into the production machine and become assets instead of remaining liabilities.
What do we find in the minister's budget? What do we find his policies portend for this reshaping process? Obviously, the most important thing in reshaping, repolishing and retooling our human resources is a vastly increased public investment in education and in technical training in order to prepare these people so that they may play their part in society, a vast public investment that would remove at least some of the conditions of abject poverty which make the possibility of these people being able to absorb an education very remote.
What do we find our government doing? The minister tells us he is going to cut his own government's spending. He is going to urge provincial and municipal governments to curtail their spending. He does this by means of exhortation and by leaving them in a rather difficult position to fulfil those functions which are largely provincial and municipal functions, education and training. For instance, he is not prepared to remove the 11 per cent sales tax to encourage and enable municipalities or school boards to increase their social capital as a basis for reshaping these presently defective units of our popultaion.
He tells us of the need for higher productivity and almost in the next breath he tells us of two steps he is taking which appear to be in the opposite direction. The minister says he is not going on with the development of the structures laboratory at the National Research Council. In the light of the tragic accident that occurred on Elgin Street yesterday I would think the folly of this type of curtailment would be underlined. In the next paragraph the minister says he is going to curtail investment in the experimental farm stations. Again, one would presume this project was designated to increase productivity.
April 1, 1966	COMMONS
These are two comparatively minor instances which illustrate the minister's reversal of his position. He says we need higher productivity and then takes steps to curtail our ability to achieve it. These are sins of commission, rather minor ones perhaps and not significant, but they are nothing like the sins of omission which must have much wider effect than the two small sins of commission I have mentioned. He ignores the existence of this large proportion of our labour force, 3.5 per cent, and blandly tells us that despite that we are near the end of the full utilization of our resources. We are faced with this fact, Mr. Speaker, that he possibly had to take this position because of past negligence on the part of this and former governments. As a result of this, he would not now be in a very good position to inaugurate any policy to reshape or retool these defective parts of our population.
To the best of my knowledge there has been no survey made by this government or previous governments as to the skills that will be required in the rapidly changing economy in which we live today. There has been no survey to find out what skills will be called for by the vast technological changes that are taking place continually. There has been no research, no surveys to the best of my knowledge with regard to the skills, capacities or qualities of those who are presently unemployed. We do not know, therefore, what we need from them.

Yes, if I have time I do not mind.
No survey has been made at all and consequently the government has tied its own hands when it comes to launching an effective program in the war against poverty. There is no doubt the recent war against poverty has become a byword in this country for a piece of government whitewashing. We do not know what skills are needed. We do
DEBATES	3733
The Budget-Mr. C. Cameron not know what capacities the unemployed have. No survey has been made, so what do we do? We sweep them under the rug. We do not include them in our potential resources utilization of which the minister tells us is reaching very close to the limit.
Of course, we have a new department recently appointed to achieve this, and I refer to the proposed ministry of manpower. I wonder how this new department will work when it comes up against the brick wall of some of the other policies of the minister? I have noticed in the minister's budget that he appears to be determined to accentuate a trend in investment in Canada which has created this situation and which, if continued much longer, must inevitably be disastrous. For the last five years at least there has been a growing disparity between investment in social capital and investment in private business capital. In 1961, 41.7 per cent of our total investment went into social capital and 58.3 per cent into business capital. By 1965 it had reached the point that 39.7 per cent was in social capital and 60.3 per cent in business capital. In the forecast produced by the Department of Trade and Commerce for 1966 we find that it is estimated that for the ensuing year the investment in social capital will have dropped to 38.4 per cent and the estimate of business investment will have risen to 62 per cent.
This, I suggest, sir, is a shocking and dangerous trend when we have reports on all hands of the failures and inadequacies of our educational system, when we have reports on all hands of the failure to provide adequate health services for the Canadian people to maintain them in the state of health that is reauired to sustain them as useful members of our society, when continually both business and government bewail the fact that we have a shortage of skilled personnel, when we have disgraceful slums in every city of the country, when we have poverty which is the breeding ground of crime and delinquency, and the non-utility of human beings as productive organisms.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
Knowing this, what do we find? We find that the government is determined to allow this disparity in investment to continue. The government is determined to allow the shortages in social capital from which we suffer today to remain. The government does not wish to take steps at all to correct this imbalance that might start us at least on the
April 1, 1966

The Budget-Mr. C. Cameron path toward solving the problem of the usefulness of human beings in modern society.
It is true, I acknowledge, that the minister is proposing to place a curb on business investment. I would imagine the minister took one hesitating, rather timid look at what they are doing in Sweden and that he felt he had to do something of the same sort. Of course, the difference is so great that it is not merely a difference in degree but a difference in kind between what the minister is suggesting and what the Swedish authorities have instituted for several years past. In that connection let me say, Mr. Speaker, that while I think the 5 per cent refundable tax is a very faltering step, if it is the forerunner of more decisive action in this field it is to be welcomed.
I noted with interest the position of the spokesman for the Progressive Conservative party when he protested against business having to relinquish $250 million, on which it is going to draw 5 per cent, without a word being said about the $140 million that is going to be taken out of the taxpayers' pockets for which they will get no return and no interest.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It has to be paid.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It has to be paid. I thought that what the spokesman for the Progressive Conservatives said was very interesting because it indicates clearly the concern of the Official Opposition with a certain section of our society. To take money from business is, of course, the ultimate sin for Conservatives.
Let us compare what the minister is doing with what they are doing in Sweden. I have here a copy of the Harvard Business Review, which outlines the Swedish program. We find there that any Swedish corporation may allocate, at its own discretion and with no necessity for government permission, up to 40 per cent of its pre-tax income to an investment reserve for economic stabilization. The amount so set aside is a deduction from income for purposes of income tax. In every case 40 per cent of the amount allocated to the investment reserve must be sterilized by deposit to the corporation's credit with the Riksbank, the Swedish central bank. There is no sterilization of the remaining 60 per cent of the investment reserve. It must be charged on the books as a reserve but it remains in the corporation's hands as part of its working capital, similar to a reserve for depreciation or for bad debts.

The important part is this: While no government permission is required to allocate funds to the reserve, control over the taxpayers' reserve is largely in the hands of the government. Control is not exercised by the revenue administration but by the Labour Market Board, a government agency, whose primary duty is to combat unemployment. I would assume, Mr. Speaker, that that board has before it the results of the sort of survey that this government has never done. I would imagine that the Labour Market Board of Sweden has a very clear idea of the skills required in every part of their society, most of which they have today achieved.
In our own instance what do we have? We have a 5 per cent refundable tax on which we are going to pay 5 per cent interest. It is not going to have any flexibility as to the time of release. The minister must release the money at the end of 18 or 36 months regardless of the state of the economy. In fact, as a weapon for stabilizing investment it would seem to me to be of very minor effect and of minor use.
It may be, as I say, that it is one first, faltering step in the direction of rational control of investment programs and policies of Canada. If so, it is a very timid one. I suggest to the minister that he should perhaps borrow from his predecessor some of his rashness, some of his panache, and I suggest that he take bolder steps in that direction.
I have noticed that the minister has boasted, not merely on this occasion but on other occasions, that we are enjoying the longest period of economic expansion in our history. No doubt we have almost reached the new millenium. Perhaps we have. If that is the case, then we have a grim outlook before us.

We have a grim outlook before us when in a period of unexampled and unprecedented economic expansion, 25 per cent of the people still are categorized as living on the borderline of poverty, when we have still
365,000	unemployed persons, when the old age pensioner is receiving $75 a month. A retired civil servant telephoned me today to tell me of the plight of a friend of hers, also a retired civil servant, whom she found living on shredded wheat for a week waiting for the pension cheque to come. If this is what the longest unprecedented sustained period of economic expansion gives us, then I say the outlook is extremely grim, and I say that we

should take another look at the policies which have created this longest unprecedented spell of economic expansion.

speechtext:
As I said before the luncheon recess, Mr. Speaker, I propose to move a subamendment to the amendment placed before the house by the official opposition. I do so now. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"and to meet the needs of taxpayers by changing the income tax structure so that single persons up to $1500 and married persons up to $3000 will not be required to pay income tax, or to meet the needs of Canadians whose incomes are below the income tax exemption levels by providing a guaranteed annual income."
The problem to which the subamendment calls attention is connected closely with what I was saying earlier in the debate. It is further proof of the inability of an unplanned market economy to distribute the fruits of expansion. Not only are we unable to distribute the fruits of our production but we place a levy on those in our society who can least afford to contribute to the operation of our economy.
I was speaking earlier of the curious manner in which the Minister of Finance had dismissed the 365,000 unemployed by making no mention of them and by suggesting at the same time that we had nearly full employment of all our resources. I suggest this is a situation which will continue to get worse. There can be no doubt that if those presently
DEBATES	3735
The Budget-Mr. C. Cameron unemployed, as appears to be the case, are unfit to perform a productive function in our society, the level of unfitness will continue to rise in line with the technological development which is taking place today, and more and more people will find themselves in this category of being unused and unuseful members of our society.
The level of usefulness, if I can use that term, is bound to climb and much more drastic steps will be required to cope with the situation than either the minister or the government have indicated up to the present. This is one of the big paradoxes of our present method of operating our society. It is the dilemma of the unplanned market economy that not only does it fail to distribute the fruits of production in an equitable manner but that it is similarly unable to allocate resources in a socially desirable way, since the only consideration affecting the allocation of those resources is that of profit. The curious thing is that the richer we become, the more quickly we approach the full use of our economic, natural and human resources, the more difficult it is for us to make sure that those who need it most are able to share in the new wealth production. This, I submit, will always be the case as long as we continue to operate on an unplanned market economic basis.
I believe the almost obsessive concern with the rate of economic growth is actually an escape mechanism to enable us to avoid this problem of equitable distribution. It stems from a social philosophy which regards organized society as merely a productive and consumptive machine and human beings as being merely an attachment to that machine.
It is true we must have growth in order to keep pace with the rising population. But it may very well be that a better allocation of our resources and a better distribution of the fruits of our society would be sufficient to provide us with decent and satisfactory lives instead of our present course which is a mad scramble to use up resources, destroy our environment, exploit the capacities of human beings and keep the machine going at any cost.
We are confronted today with a foretaste of what will be done to us in more acute form by the automation and cybernation which awaits us. The time is fast approaching when we shall be obliged to take a hard look at the philosophy of human purpose which we now have, and at the philosophy of organizing

ourselves for the production and distribution of resources. I have always felt that in a modern state the goal of civilized state should be that of developing as far as possible an egalitarian society. I am not suggesting, here, any counsel of perfection; indeed, if that were possible, it might not be desirable.
We still have an immense number who are incentives. We have heard a lot about that this morning from the Official Opposition. I agree there must be incentives which will induce people to undertake the rigorous and lengthy training and education required to fill the most skilled positions in our society. But incentives used merely to encourage people to seek the most profitable places for investment land us in the state in which we find ourselves today where, in spite of the long and unprecedented economic growth, 25 per cent of our people are still living near poverty level.

We still have an immense number who are living in stringent circumstances and on whom, apparently, we must impose taxes. We still have old people, retired civil servants and disabled people living at substandard levels, and we still have a totally defective educational machine in this country incapable of producing the very productive force that the Minister of Finance tells us we must have.
Therefore I suggest we should not look merely at statistics. Statistics do not give us the real picture of our egalitarian society. We hear no mention of all the extra income acquired by those who happen to be in a position of prosperity. We hear no mention of the man who has a $50,000 home and who draws considerable income from the fact that he lives in this home and enjoys its amenities. He does not get taxed on that. I suggest that until some future government recognizes that we must divorce the idea of livelihood from that of a piece of machinery in a large productive machine we are going to have this continual trouble. We are going to continue to the point of expanding our economy and then being told that, because we are in an inflationary position, we cannot provide larger pensions for old people, and provide education as it should be provided, and cannot reduce income tax levels because we need the revenues.

This is because the whole of our society is geared to the production of profits, to the maldistribution of wealth in order that those who own and operate the productive forces of society may draw their first tribute from it and leave us the rest. If this continues we are going to have more throw-outs because of technological changes, but somehow we will have to achieve some means of distributing the wealth that automation and cybernation have made possible. This is one of the great opportunities for mankind, but if we are going to have the sort of program presented by the Minister of Finance in his budget we are going to lose that opportunity and from our wealth possibilities we are going to create more and more misery for more and more people.

So, they consult their economists. The first one replies; well, we shall build factories and they will manufacture hats. No, says the second one, we shall cut off heads and then there will be enough hats. That is exactly what our Minister of Finance has done in his 1966 budget. He cut off heads, he cut down the number of public works, and he asked the provinces to do as much. He also asked the industrial and manufacturing interests to cut down on their investments.
Everything is in progress, but man no longer knows what to do with progress. There are too many heads? Let us cut them off. Too much progress? Let us try and restrict it.
That is not the way to develop a country, Mr. Speaker. One never develops the economy of a country or the country itself by trying to limit its growth but by encouraging it.

Mr. Speaker, there are in fact two problems facing the country today, or so it seems according to the speech made by the minister.
First, there is the increase in the cost of living. Second, our balance of payments shows a deficit.
The increase in the cost of living, where does it come from and for what reason? Almost everyone tries to hide it from himself and the hon. Minister of Finance especially refuses to see it. But the reason for the increased cost of living during the last year or two is mostly the increase in taxes.

When a province increases taxes by 2 per cent, prices go up 2 per cent. When there is a 1.8 per cent or 1.9 per cent tax increase, as there was last year, prices go up. When the employer is also forced to pay 1.8 or 1.9 per cent more, prices rise. When an 11 per cent tax is charged on building materials, prices inevitably go up.
Through the creation of all sorts of new taxes, we have come to the point where the businessman, simply to make his reports to the government on pensions, health unemployment insurance, income tax for his employees, deductions at the source, taxes on profits, personal income tax, etc., has to hire a whole staff of accountants, secretaries and assistants to figure out all those things and divide everything according to each department. You can imagine that this increases production costs for industrialists and manufacturers contributes to increase prices.
Taxes are the main factor of the rise in the cost of living at this time. The minister complains that the cost of living is on the rise. But he is the first one responsible, for it is not the opposition which raises taxes, but rather the Minister of Finance who decides such things. And as this is the primary cause of inflation, the man responsible for inflation in Canada is the Minister of Finance every time he makes a decision to increase taxes.
Today whether you want it or not, there is 47 cents worth of tax in everything you buy. Every dollar's worth of products includes 47 cents in various taxes, either income, municipal, provincial, school or other tax. In every dollar's worth of production, there are 47 cents in taxes.
The minister wonders what inflation stems from. It stems from taxes or levies, which are higher here in Canada than anywhere else.
The second problem the country has to face is that of the balance of payments. Let us note this however: if we have a deficit, it is not that our exports are inferior to our imports. On the contrary, they are greater than our imports, but over and above that, huge amounts of money go out of the country in dividends, profits and interests paid to foreign companies. That is what causes the deficit in our balance of payments because, as a matter of fact, if we consider only the value of products we ship outside this country and those we bring in, our exports exceed our imports, but we have to pay the tax on money sent to foreign investors who develop our natural resources because we never had a government that could do it.

There is no mention of increasing family allowances and old age pensions, or of raising tax deductions to $1,500 or $3,000, as was suggested by our colleagues of the New Democratic Party. We find their amendment is satisfactory and we are going to vote for it.
As for the Conservative amendment, it seems to us satisfactory at first sight. I did not have the opportunity to consider it thoroughly, but at first glance it seems satisfactory and, as far as we are concerned, we shall also vote for it.
